comments.author: staticdrift
comments.text: The section on interchange symbols is great, but the piece undersells the real constraint: transit type has to survive being read at a 30 degree angle, through scratched polycarbonate, by someone in motion who is mildly panicking. Every "beautiful" map I've seen fail in the field failed at exactly this.

replies.author: helveticat
replies.text: OP here — completely agree, and it's why the article spends so long on x-height and counter apertures. A gorgeous geometric sans with closed counters turns to mush behind scratched plastic. The ugliest map in my survey was also the most legible from a moving escalator.

replies.author: staticdrift
replies.text: The escalator test should be an industry standard. Print the candidate map, tape it to a wall, walk past it briskly while looking for a specific minor station. Repeat until humbled.

comments.author: lambdacurious
comments.text: Tangent: the same legibility-under-stress constraints show up in aviation cockpit typography and, weirdly, in terminal fonts. Somebody should write the unified theory of "type for people who cannot afford to squint."

comments.author: kerningpair
comments.text: Pedantic but important: several of the specimens shown aren't the fonts the agencies specify, they're the fonts the sign shops actually had. Anyone who has audited a real transit system knows the official style guide and the platform signage diverge within one procurement cycle.

replies.author: offbyfun
replies.text: The signage equivalent of config drift. Somewhere there is a station sign that is the typographic version of a hand-edited production server.
